national.title: This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
national.summary: This year's the Princess Diana honor roll highlights 198 inspiring young activists and advocates — including an 18-year-old guy in India who founded Team Period.
national.body:
Aadvik Jain (third from right) has won a Princess Diana award for starting Team Period to counter menstrual stigma. He's standing with other members of this activist group and teacher Sonia Rao (center, in green sari). "Our work would not be possible without her guidance and support," he says. Team Period hide caption

Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?

At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.

This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.

Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.

Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.

And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.

Aadvik Jain, founder of Team Period, plans to study medicine and public health in Italy next year. Team Period hide caption

national.title: Paraguay's president under house arrested after bank collapse
national.summary: The president was placed under house arrest after being removed from office following the collapse of a bank linked to the government.
national.body: Paraguay's president has been placed on house arrest on Friday after the collapse of a government-linked bank that locked nearly half the country's population out of their accounts.Paraguay's Senate voted to remove Santiago Peña for misconduct in office, making him the second president ousted by impeachment since the end of Gen. Alfredo Stroessner's 35-year dictatorship in 1989.Regulators had seized Ueno Bank just three days earlier, sending shock waves through the financial system and setting off the country's worst political crisis in more than a decade.Peña was ordered to remain at one of his homes in Asunción until he appears before prosecutors Saturday morning on charges of breach of trust, influence peddling and using public office for personal gain, the most serious of which carry up to 10 years in prison. Lawmakers accuse him of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.The Paraguayan president denied wrongdoing.When regulators seized the bank, Ueno customers could no longer withdraw cash, access their savings or use their cards to buy anything. The digital lender had aggressively courted the poor and unbanked with generous supermarket rebates, and more than 1 million Paraguayans opened their first bank account there, according to Ueno. Even players on the national soccer team, which Ueno sponsored through its run to a World Cup upset of Germany this year, say they can't reach their money.The fallout has spread well beyond savers. A ride-hailing app that relied on Ueno shut down, leaving 3,000 drivers without work. The state power company says $21 million in loans from the Inter-American Development Bank and Taiwan, earmarked for public works, is trapped at the bank. Paraguay's bonds have posted some of the worst losses in emerging markets this week, and the guaraní has slid against the dollar.Some depositors began recovering their money Thursday, starting with those holding up to 10 million guaraníes (about $1,500). Deposits are insured up to about $35,000, which the central bank says covers 97% of Ueno's customers. It calls the collapse an isolated case and insists the broader financial system is safe.

national.title: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
national.summary: Thousands across the U.S. have gotten involved to oppose data centers. One is a Maryland woman who'd been evicted after a pay cut and became a leader of a community effort that blocked a vast project.
national.body:
Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active in the opposition to the possible data center at the site of the demolished Landover Mall in Prince George's County, less than a mile from where she lived. If the project is built, the development could occupy more than 80 acres. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.

In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.

"I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."

Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.

Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.

"It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."

They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.

national.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
national.summary: There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
national.body:
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.

"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.

"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.

Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.

national.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
national.summary: The 82-year-old appeared in court in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented.
national.body:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".

In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.

At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.

No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

national.title: Paraguay's president impeached and under house arrest after bank collapse
national.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.
national.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.

He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.

Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.

The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.

Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.

"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.

national.title: Pope in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
national.summary: Pope Leo travels to Uruguay just three weeks after having surgery for lung cancer.
national.body:
Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.

The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.

The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.

The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru , which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop.

"I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay.

"Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.

Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.

On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.

national.title: How 2 lifelong singles in the same town ended up married
national.summary: Al Sager, 65, and Susan Guc, 76, had both been happily single for decades. Then they met in the most surprising way, and everything changed.
national.body: For his entire life, 65-year-old Al Sager of Bay City, Michigan, had been single."You see relationships sour and it's like, 'Nah, I don't want that,'" Sager told CBS News. "â¦ I was alone, but I wasn't lonely." Across town, meanwhile, 76-year-old Susan Guc felt the same. "If there would be anybody out there, who would I really want?" Guc said. As it turned out, the answer was nobody. "And I was happy with that," she said. "I really was."Guc worked as a nurse devoted solely to her patients. Sager was a truck driver who was always on the road. They were two of Bay City's most committed "uncommitteds."Until this week, when they were married. All those years of singlehood came to a surprising end, leaving relatives in disbelief."We were all just shocked," one relative said. "I about fell out of my chair," said another. "I didn't expect that." Guc explained: "It was just a fluke."It all began a couple of years ago, according to Guc, when they both underwent heart procedures and were placed in the same cardiac rehab program.Guc was on a treadmill when she noticed Sager on an exercise bike. He didn't notice anything, but she really liked his smile.He was oblivious to her, so she hit him with a rock â literally. The rock had the word "smile" etched on it. "Yes, she threw a rock at me to get my attention," Sager said. "This rock rocked," Guc said.Actually, she more like handed it to him, but it did knock him for a loop. "I thought she was trying to tell me, 'Hey, you don't smile enough,'" Sager said. "â¦ And I said, 'Well, I better look into this more.'"Today, Sager and Guc are all smiles and beaming a message to anyone out there who thinks they're too old to find their person."I had thought that, but look what happened to me," Guc said. Added Sager, "Oh, absolutely, it's never too late."

California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request.The case was at the forefront of the Trump administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Mr. Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence.On Monday, on the eve of Election Day, the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal from the Justice Department to require California to separate mail ballots received from the approximately 20,000 people it alleged were noncitizens. The Justice Department remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what it says are suspected noncitizens. national.summary: Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations.
national.body: Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. national.title: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
national.summary: Jehovah's Witness leaders relaxed strict rules on blood transfusions, but the change came 23 days too late for Isaac Valdez.
national.body:
In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.

He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.

Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.

As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.

But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.

The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.

A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.

His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.

national.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
national.summary: For some tourists, the contrast between Somalia's reputation and what they experience on the ground can be striking.
national.body:
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.

This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.

Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.

Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.

"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.

But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.

Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.

Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.

national.title: Cornell faculty pass no-confidence vote over leadership's handling of Jane Doe allegations
national.summary: Friday's resolution by academic staff is largely symbolic as they do not have the power to remove those in charge of the university.
national.body:
Cornell University's academic staff have passed a vote of no confidence over its leadership's handling of what staff call a "crisis of sexual assault" after a former student alleged she was gang raped while attending.

The woman, known anonymously as Jane Doe, is suing her former university and the fraternity over an alleged incident involving several men at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

All seven of the accused have denied wrongdoing when contacted by the BBC's US partner CBS. None has been charged with a crime.

Friday's no-confidence vote passed by 75 votes to 50. It is largely symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the power to remove leaders.

The resolution states that the faculty senate, which represents academic staff, "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University".

It did not make any specific recommendations or suggest what administrators did wrong in response to the accusation.

It is a rebuke of university leaders including President Michael Kotlikoff, whom Doe has accused of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident.

The Ivy League institution in upstate New York has said her account of Kotlikoff's reaction is "incorrect".

It includes financial records for the president, vice president and more than 100 White House staffers, including Susie Wiles and Stephen Miller. CBS News uses an automated system to monitor ethics disclosures across the government, including those posted on the White House page. The system checks for new filings every 30 minutes. national.title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
national.summary: The US president's promotion of Miller, a loyal partisan firebrand to be his new chief of staff sets up likely clashes with Congress.
national.body:
North America correspondent Published 6 November 2026 In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.

On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.

"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."

Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.

He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.

national.title: Razor-tight Mississippi Senate race sparks ballot battle - could there be a recount?
national.summary: Lawyers for both campaigns in Mississippi's US Senate race are preparing for a possible legal battle as the close count continues.
national.body:
The Democrats hold a narrow lead over the Republicans in the US Senate race in Mississippi, with both sides in a dispute over the counting of the remaining votes which could decide the outcome.

Lawyers for each campaign are preparing for a possible legal battle over the final results and weighing in on the examination of ballots.

The result could mark the end of almost 40 years of Republican control over Mississippi's senate seats and will determine the size of the Democrats' majority in the upper house.

Mississippi is the only US state which does not have a set procedure in place to trigger a recount - and the pressure is on to declare a winner with the state's 13 November deadline for certification approaching.

With 97% of the votes counted as of Friday, Democratic candidate Scott Colom is about 2,500 votes ahead of the incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Mississippi's Secretary of State Michael Watson said on Wednesday that 3,600 "absentee-by-mail ballots" were still to be counted. The state can accept these votes so long as they were postmarked by election day and are received by 10 November.

Watson said there are also an "unknown" number of provisional ballots, also known as affidavit ballots, to be counted. These are typically cast when a voter lacked the required identification to cast their vote. The deadline for voters to resolve any ID issues with provisional ballots, usually by providing acceptable photo identification, is also 10 November.

Mississippi Republican Party Chair Michael Hurst said on Thursday that they estimated there could be "approximately 20,000 outstanding ballots left to be counted".

national.title: Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests
national.summary: Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.
national.body:
Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press

Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press

GENEVA (AP) — People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.

The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China.

Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands.

The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies.

"It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern.

national.title: Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida jet crash says her final radio calls showed 'she's tough'
national.summary: "I wanted to be by her side," Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach his daughter to fly, said at a news conference Friday, at times holding back tears. "Inside the plane. To help."
national.body:
The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot who died along with eight others when their Learjet crashed in Florida said Friday he has listened to his daughter's heartbreaking final radio transmissions "many times" since the crash.

Allan Filgueiras, a pilot who helped teach his daughter to fly, was searching for answers as to why the plane plunged from the sky on Sunday. Instead, he found immense pride in how his daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, handled the crisis.

"I did listen to that many times trying to find a clue. In my head. How'd that happen? And wow, she's tough," Allan Filgueiras said at a news conference Friday.

"I wanted to be by her side," he said, at times holding back tears. "Inside the plane. To help."

In her conversation with air traffic control, Nathalia Filgueiras can first be heard calmly reporting ice buildup on the plane as it flew into a thunderstorm and turbulence tossed it up and down by 700 feet (200 meters). The situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. "Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!" she said.

Her father and aviation safety experts are impressed that Filgueiras continued to call out updates on what was happening even as she realized the plane's fate was sealed.

"For the family — it's like having the heart torn from my chest," her father said in Spanish. "I have to find a way to go on living."

The family wants to push back against online criticism over whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a high-performance business jet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot's license and get certified for a Learjet. The plane's captain, 55-year-old Jeff Gregory, is believed to have been at the controls in the aircraft's final minutes.

national.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
national.summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
national.body:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user , external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise , external " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date , external " in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

For generations of Newfane families, a trip to Bob Eadie’s Barbershop was about more than getting a haircut. It was a chance to catch up, share a story and spend time with a man who became part of the fabric of the community. After 67 years behind the chair, Eadie has retired, closing a chapter on a business and a hometown legacy built one haircut at a time.

Robert Eadie moved from Clearfield, Pennsylvania, to Newfane when he was 12. As a teenager looking to find his place in a new community, he was quickly drawn to attending many of the high school athletic games — football, basketball, and wrestling. He also found his foot in the door at Bill Murphy’s Barbershop, where his first job and opportunity in the barbering profession began as a cleaner. At about 16 years of age, Bill asked Bob if he would like an apprenticeship position at the shop. There were three other apprentices at that time. The apprenticeships were state-regulated and emphasized sanitation, clipper work, and razor techniques. Once he completed his apprenticeship, he became a partner with Mr. Murphy. After graduation, Bob married his high school sweetheart, Sheila, and by 1961 they welcomed their firstborn. At just 19 years old, he quickly learned perseverance and the meaning of hard work.

local.body:
FALCONER -- Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton's offense has been a work in progress all season.

That unit is taking the Eagles to the Section VI Class C final.

Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton, Class C South's No. 3 seed, allowed just 68 yards rushing and stopped both of Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove's trips inside the red zone to beat the Herd 14-0 in a semifinal Friday night at Bill Race Field.

"It was pretty evident early on in the season that defensively we were going to be pretty tough. ... If we're being honest, the defense has really carried us for the better part of the season. (Chris) Payne has done a tremendous job as always," Harper said of his longtime defensive coordinator. "You can count on it: death, taxes and Chris Payne's defense."

The win sends the defending sectional champions into next Friday's 2 p.m. title game against Barker/Royalton-Hartland at the University at Buffalo's Broadview Stadium. The Bulls, Class C North's top seed, beat Clymer/Sherman/Panama 24-20 in Friday's other semifinal.

"They are big. They are physical. They have a great back," Harper said of Barker/Royalton-Hartland. "They don't really do anything fancy. They get into a stack-I and they are going to run the ball right at you. That's tough to stop."

Chautauqua Lake/Westfield/Brocton didn't shine offensively in Falconer -- Tristen Gibbs led the Eagles with 21 carries for 109 yards -- but the Eagles did force three turnovers and stop Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove on downs three other times.

"Chris Payne did a great job. If there was a Player of the Game, it would have been Chris Payne for preparing them really well," Falconer/Cassadaga Valley/Maple Grove head coach Curt Fischer said. "He's a great coach and I have a lot of respect for him."

local.title: Dunkirk chief offers reassurance on BESS
local.summary: Battery Energy Storage Systems do offer unique hazards, Dunkirk Fire Chief Nicholas Barter said last week. However, as he pointed out, “Everything has risk — everything we do.” BESS discussion was the highlight of a talk Barter gave to Revitalize Dunkirk’s quarterly meeting. “At some point, it’s goi
local.body:
Battery Energy Storage Systems do offer unique hazards, Dunkirk Fire Chief Nicholas Barter said last week. However, as he pointed out, "Everything has risk -- everything we do."

BESS discussion was the highlight of a talk Barter gave to Revitalize Dunkirk's quarterly meeting.

"At some point, it's going to be here," he said. "I'm going to recognize that for what it is, at the scale of a community and a hazard we have to plan for."

The systems store varying amounts of power from the electric grid, for release in times of high demand. "We've been working with developers because we have concerns as well," Barter said.

"There is definitely a risk with them -- but it is projected to everyone's mind by high profile incidents," he said. Barter mentioned a major January 2025 fire in Moss Landing, California, that prompted evacuations. The fire briefly rekindled in September during cleanup operations.

However, he noted, every BESS is different -- and part of what led to and worsened the Moss Landing fire was the enclosure of storage arrays in a concrete building. The two BESS proposals for Dunkirk would be open-air. One of the proposals is approved for currently unused land several hundred yards from Brigham Road, another is sought closer to the same road but not approved.

Barter said his department will approach open-air BESS fires with the attitude of, "It's almost let it burn."

He acknowledged that is an unusual tactic, but said it is occasionally used with chemical fires. "It does sound bad, but there is a plan out there."

local.title: Voters took control of misguided U.S. leadership
local.summary: What an election! Folks, the power has always been ours, we just need to be convinced to use it! local.body:
What an election! Folks, the power has always been ours, we just need to be convinced to use it! For every election, large or small, we should have a very modest expectation that at least a majority of registered voters would cast a ballot. I heard so many folks at the polls say this, that if you don't vote, don't complain. These people take their responsibility seriously, as we all should.

Not every country affords its citizens the right and privilege of a say in its government, and we are lucky to be where we are, and to be part of this blue wave that is rising to the occasion. This nation was founded on the principles of government of, by, and for, the people. Without the "by" there isn't a "for" for long. We must not take that responsibility lightly.

Up until Tuesday, our future as a democratic country was in jeopardy. Tuesday's election results grabbed us back from the precipice of autocracy - for now. But it shouldn't have taken this long, so much damage has been done to our beloved country and its citizens, so much greed, corruption, hatred, ignoring of the common good of the people.

The plan to take the reins of government away from the people and give them to the huge corporate CEOs, to put big business interests in charge of us, to make us feudal peasants to the moneyed class, was taken from the pages of history and put into the pages of Project 2025. If we can build on the momentum that this election has given us, we may see this plan unravel. Trump was useful to the Project while things were going well, now they may not be too happy with him either. We may see rats jumping ship. We may see Elon go try to ply his influence elsewhere. We can only hope. We the people must stay strong.

Remember, our votes are what puts the politicians where they are. If we just let them go their merry way without holding them accountable to us, how many of them will stay true to their campaign promises? Very few. It takes strong character, an internal honesty and integrity, and if that is not something they have carried with them since their childhood, it is very easy for them to make excuses and to follow the shiny objects of wealth and power. We have to keep them in line, be strict parents, and we have not been doing a good job lately. They need to know we are paying attention.

For instance, just a factual five-minute biography read on DJT would have told every voter all they needed to know about his real-life history and why to avoid electing him at all costs. But so many chose not to take the time, to listen to his snake-oil pitch (remember the story about the snake he always liked to tell - that was him revealing his truth, just as clear as day), and believe his made-up reality showbiz persona. It was so much more fun to go to his rallies, to laugh at his nonsense, to feel authenticated in the grievances that he assured his followers were the fault of Obama, or Biden, or their next-door neighbor- anything to take away the pain of responsibility rather than work toward a way to fix them. We all were warned, now we have to claw our way back from the ruination that he inevitably caused, – that was predicted by everything he has done his entire life.

NEWFANE -- Less than six minutes into its semifinal matchup at No. 2 Newfane, the Silver Creek/Forestville football team was already down by two scores. The 3-seeded Black Knights chased the defending-champion Panthers all game and Newfane raced to a 44-20 victory in the Section VI Class D semifinals on Friday night.

The opening kickoff spelled doom for the Black Knights as a line drive kick could not be handled and Newfane recovered to score only three plays later when Nasir Spencer broke free for a 20-yard touchdown.

Trailing 8-0 early, Silver Creek/Forestville did not have much of an answer when it did receive the following kickoff as it went three and out. Newfane then promptly worked into Silver Creek/Forestville territory and Spencer rattled off a 19-yard run to put the Panthers up 14-0.

Silver Creek/Forestville was down, but certainly not out as it showed on the next drive. Working with a short field, Manny Sanchez made it even shorter when he broke off a 45-yard run down to the Newfane 10.

The Panthers would not allow the Black Knights to reach the end zone easily as it was 4th-and-5 when Will Duliba rolled out on the play-action pass to find Dom Anders for the 5-yard touchdown pass. Anders followed up catching the two-point conversion and Silver Creek/Forestville had something to build on.

While the offense found its footing, the Silver Creek/Forestville defense could not stop the Newfane attack and the Panthers finally ran some time off the clock on a drive which they eventually finished in the second quarter. Instead of Spencer on the ground, quarterback Jesse Hughey connected with Mikey Henning for a 27-yard touchdown pass and Jake Morello's run made it a 22-8 score.

local.title: Measles outbreak defies advances in medicine
local.summary: My medical training didn’t prepare me for this moment. I grew up in Warren County, Pa., but now live in Buffalo and work as a hospitalist, meaning If you become a patient at the hospital and have to stay overnight or are not going straight to surgery, I am often one of the doctors taking […]
local.body:
I grew up in Warren County, Pa., but now live in Buffalo and work as a hospitalist, meaning If you become a patient at the hospital and have to stay overnight or are not going straight to surgery, I am often one of the doctors taking care of you.

I recently went to speak at a conference in Lancaster, Pa., at the center of the current largest U.S. outbreak of measles, which claimed its sixth death this past week. As I prepared for that trip, I found myself pondering how to reduce my exposure.

I worried, not for myself, but for my beloved (and fully vaccinated) toddler and aging parents who love to visit their grandchild. Current vaccine guidance says my childhood vaccines likely protect me, but immunity is not always perfect, and I was headed to a high-risk area. Should I repeat my vaccination?

If you had told me in medical school (11 years ago) that I would have to plan for patients with vaccine-preventable diseases which had previously been almost completely eliminated in the United States, I would not have believed you.

I have previously written about the importance of COVID and flu vaccinations. Now I must discuss the childhood vaccination schedule as well, as people in prominent positions of leadership continue to undermine evidence and diminish the confidence people once had in vaccines.

We see real-time consequences as outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases appear across the country. They are not caused by immigrant communities, undocumented or otherwise (as one myth claims), but by American communities where vaccinations have decreased. I was glad to see several Warren-area medical professionals (including my father, a now-retired pediatrician) sign a statement encouraging vaccinations and emphasizing their importance in public health.

Some people have claimed that doctors are not taught about vaccines, which is false. We all experience a pediatrics rotation, learn about diseases vaccines prevent, and study basics of vaccine components. Still, over the past six years I have looked at vaccine inserts and ingredients with much greater scrutiny, to explain them better to people via social media and to understand what my family and I receive. I am grateful for the plethora of vaccine and disease research making that work possible.

Yet my medical training did not anticipate this. So I think about the toddler here and his grandparents in Warren, and how vaccines help us protect ourselves and also protect the vulnerable around us.

local.title: 'Marriage is a gift': Officer shot 6 times celebrates the wedding he almost missed
local.summary: Five months after Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst was shot six times while responding to a call, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée, Haley.
local.body: Five months after Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst was shot six times while responding to a domestic violence call, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée, Haley."I'm just so thankful, you know, that we are celebrating our marriage on Friday and my family and my fiancée is not mourning the loss of me," Hurst said in an interview earlier this week.Hurst was responding to a call about a violent domestic May 26 near Broadway and Sherman Street when he was shot."One officer shot. Every available to Sherman," a dispatcher could be heard saying over police radio.Hurst was struck six times and rushed to ECMC.One of Hurst's friends in the police department called Haley with the news."I was like, 'You need to tell me what's going on,'" Haley recalled. "And he said that Marc had been shot."At first, she didn't know how serious his injuries were."I was obviously freaking out, like, he's been shot everywhere," she said.Hurst remembers realizing that despite being shot multiple times, he was still breathing and able to think."I just remember, and I believe it's just from the Lord, this overwhelming peace," Hurst said.As he focused on getting out of the house, another thought crossed his mind: his upcoming wedding."I remember being down on the ground and focusing on getting out of the house that we were in, but also being like, 'You know what? She's gonna be really ticked off if I miss this wedding.'"Hurst survived. After six days in the hospital, he walked out on his own as fellow officers gathered to see him leave.Last month, he received the City of Buffalo's Medal of Honor.Through it all, Haley has been by his side."It's been humbling and emotional," she said. "Even when I would go back and forth from the hospital to get him more clothes and everything that week, like thinking about, 'Oh my God, we still get married in a couple of months, and we almost didn't.'"Now their wedding day has arrived.Hurst said surviving the shooting has changed the way he looks at moments that might otherwise seem ordinary, from watching his nieces walk down the aisle to seeing family and friends gathered together.And then there will be the moment he sees Haley."To see Haley coming down the aisle, I can't even put it into words right now, comparing to what could have been," Hurst said. local.title: NY Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie faces questions over more than $1 million in sports-related spending
local.summary: A New York Focus investigation found the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee paid for luxury sports experiences while receiving corporate donations, including from a company lobbying state lawmakers.
local.body: New York Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie faces questions about how a political committee under his control spent more than $1 million on sports-related events, including luxury suites and tickets to games involving some of the state's most popular professional sports teams.An investigation by New York Focus found the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee paid teams, stadiums and sports-related companies more than $1 million since Heastie became Assembly Speaker in 2015. The spending included events involving the New York Yankees, New York Mets, Buffalo Sabres, Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and UBS Arena.Heastie, a well-known sports fan, attended a number of those events, including a Subway Series game at Citi Field, an NBA playoff matchup at Madison Square Garden and games at Yankee Stadium.The investigation raises questions about whether the events were primarily legitimate political fundraising activities or provided personal benefits to Heastie and other political figures.The Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee's housekeeping account can accept unlimited corporate donations. However, state law restricts how that money can be spent.Housekeeping funds are intended to pay for permanent party headquarters and staff, as well as ordinary party activities that are not specifically intended to promote individual candidates.Spending that money on fundraising for the committee is permitted, and financial disclosure documents frequently listed fundraising as the expense code for the sports-related expenditures.But New York Focus reporter Sam Mellins questioned whether fundraising was always the actual goal, especially considering the photos Heastie posted on social media, posing with sports stars, friends and colleagues."Was that the primary purpose of the events, or was it primarily for the personal benefit of the politicians and the political figures involved? I don't feel 100% confident about that," Mellins said.State law prohibits campaign funds from being spent on purely personal expenses.Mellins said Heastie personally benefited from attending games in luxury suites and box seats, even if there may have been a legitimate political purpose for some of the events.One of the companies that provided significant support to the committee was Buffalo-based Delaware North.The company donated luxury suite packages, including one for a Boston Celtics game Hea

local.title: Community group fighting back after illegal dumping plagues Buffalo
local.summary: Illegal dumping has plagued private and city-owned vacant lots in Buffalo for years, and an abandoned boat now sitting at the Wonder Bread factory shows the problem isn't going away.
local.body: Illegal dumping has plagued private and city-owned vacant lots in Buffalo for years, and an abandoned boat now sitting at the Wonder Bread factory shows the problem isn't going away.I first spoke with Kevin Hayes at the East Side site back in July, after he reached out to tell me about the ongoing issue."Someone left their boat here," Hayes said. "The city hasn't taken anything away," Hayes said.The property is owned by Harry Stinson, who also owns the vacant Buffalo Grand Hotel. Fencing on Northampton Street is part of an anti-dumping pilot project. local.title: Downtown Buffalo businesses show signs of growth as new shops prepare to open
local.summary: After years of downtown businesses closing their doors, signs of a shift are showing, with some local businesses expanding and others preparing to open.
local.body: After years of downtown businesses closing their doors, signs of a shift are showing, with some local businesses expanding and others preparing to open.For customers like Esther Nyakato, the growth is something worth celebrating.Nyakato considers herself a loyal regular at Jack's Corner Cafe, where she says the food, drinks and staff keep her coming back.Jack's Corner Cafe recently reopened at 130 Genesee Street after closing its original location for nearly two weeks to move into a larger space right across the street.For employees, it means more room to serve customers and a more comfortable environment."It's amazing. I like the new space. It's so much more comfortable. We aren't on top of each other," said Zoya Amore, a barista who has worked at the cafe for five years, since it first opened.Amore said the response has been positive, with familiar customers continuing to stop in."The response has been good," she said. "We seem to have our regulars almost every day."Nyakato said the cafe's expansion reflects the support given by the community."That shows how much people love this place and are coming and seeing regulars," she said. "The people I work with also recommended this place." WATCH: Downtown Buffalo businesses show signs of growth as new shops prepare to openAnd Jack's Corner Cafe is not the only business bringing activity downtown.ERTH, a specialty Yemeni coffee shop, is expected to open in the coming weeks at The Hotel @ The Lafayette, adding another coffee option to the downtown area.Meanwhile, a new bookstore called The Walrus Said is preparing to open at 600 Main Street, near Chippewa.The new openings come as small businesses continue to navigate high costs and the challenges of operating in an evolving economic climate.For Nyakato, seeing local businesses grow is important not just for customers, but for the surrounding community."It's important to see that local businesses can flourish with the local people and basically uplift the community. It's something we can keep seeing, hopefully," she said.As more businesses look to establish themselves downtown, their investments could help shape what the next chapter looks like.

local.title: Capitol Conversations: Bureau reporters break down the latest
local.summary: New York Public News Network reporters Jon Campbell and Samuel King talk about the latest developments at the State Capitol in Albany.
local.body:
Listen • 4:11 New York Public News Network reporters Jon Campbell and Samuel King talk about the latest developments at the State Capitol in Albany.

Gov. Kathy Hochul won a resounding victory over her Republican challenger, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, in this year’s election.

The governor was able to improve her margin in all 62 counties compared to 2022 — every single one of them.

Attorney General Letitia James and Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli also won their reelection bids.

Republicans were hopeful that their messaging about Hochul and failed leadership by Democrats would counteract the national mood against President Donald Trump and Republicans but that was not the case.

Republicans also suffered losses in the state Legislature. They lost seats on Long Island, in New York City, the Capital Region and other parts of the state, which means the Democrats have regained a two-thirds supermajority in the Senate and will now have the largest majority in party history in the Assembly.

The New York Public News Network’s Jon Campbell and Samuel King discuss those developments at the Capitol.

entertainment.title: Benson Boone Brings Young Fan Battling Cancer Onstage at Brisbane Concert
entertainment.summary: “I’ve had the opportunity of meeting a 13-year-old girl who is battling her second round of cancer,” Boone told the crowd.
entertainment.body:
Benson Boone opened the Australian leg of his Wanted Man tour with a special guest. He brought a 13-year-old fan who is battling cancer onstage to sing “Beautiful Things” with him on her birthday. Explore Benson Boone See latest videos, charts and news

The moment came at the end of Boone’s set at Brisbane Entertainment Centre on Friday (Nov. 6). The Music reported that the singer stopped to introduce the final song. Related Céline Dion Plays Air Bass at Metallica's Sphere Show Lincoln Celebrated the Art of Rejuvenation at Billboard Latin Music Week Teddy Swims' 'Mr. Know It All' Hits No. 1 on Billboard Pop Airplay Chart

“I’ve had the opportunity of meeting a 13-year-old girl who is battling her second round of cancer,” Boone told the crowd, according to the outlet. “It’s her birthday today and her birthday wish was to come on stage and sing ‘Beautiful Things.’”

The fan, Kenzie Riddle, then rose from an upper platform and joined Boone on the song. According to The Music, roughly 10,000 people were in the arena.

Riddle has Ewing’s sarcoma. As reported by Nine’s Today, she believed she had beaten the illness after about two and a half years of treatment, but the cancer returned and she is now facing intensive chemotherapy. Her family said they bought tickets to the show in July as her 13th birthday present. Her campaign to meet Boone took off online after a local musician, Fergus Hogan, shared an Instagram video about her story.

“I love his energetic style and how he’s so over the top,” Riddle told Today before the concert. “He’s kinda crazy and I love it.”

Her family also told the program: “She’s such an unbelievable inspiration to so many people… But I think even bigger than that is the community behind her.”

“Beautiful Things” was Boone’s breakout single. Released in January 2024, it reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became one of the most-streamed songs in the world that year. Boone followed it with his debut album Fireworks & Rollerblades that April. His second album, American Heart , arrived in 2025 and included the single “Mystical Magical.”

entertainment.summary: The singer showed off her air-bass skills during Metallica's Life Burns Faster residency at Las Vegas' Sphere.
entertainment.body:
Céline Dion might be best known for her soaring power ballads, but the Canadian superstar proved she knows her way around a heavy metal concert, too.

The “My Heart Will Go On” singer was spotted enthusiastically playing air bass during Metallica ‘s Life Burns Faster residency at Sphere in Las Vegas on Thursday (Nov. 5), with fan-filmed footage capturing her enjoying the performance from a suite inside the venue. Related Lincoln Celebrated the Art of Rejuvenation at Billboard Latin Music Week Teddy Swims' 'Mr. Know It All' Hits No. 1 on Billboard Pop Airplay Chart Billboard Italy Women in Music 2026: All the Honorees Revealed Explore Celine Dion Guns N' Roses Metallica See latest videos, charts and news

In a video shared on Instagram by user @theordacityyy , Dion can be seen standing and mimicking the bass-playing techniques of Metallica ‘s Robert Trujillo, enthusiastically moving her hands as the musician performed alongside guitarist Kirk Hammett.

The moment occurred during the band’s customary “Kirk and Rob Doodle,” an instrumental segment that gives Hammett and Trujillo an opportunity to jam together during the show. According to the concert’s reported setlist, the Nov. 5 installment incorporated “Motown Yo Town” and “Copenhagen.”

Dion wasn’t the only famous face taking in the performance. Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash was also reportedly spotted in the suite, while members of No Doubt were among the other musicians seen enjoying the concert.

Although Dion’s enthusiasm might seem unexpected to fans more familiar with her romantic ballads, her appreciation for Metallica is hardly newEarlier this year, the five-time Grammy winner shared a selection of songs from her personal playlist , which included Metallica’s 1996 single “Until It Sleeps.”

“Eddy, one of my twins, his favorite band is Metallica,” Dion said in the video, before enthusiastically attempting her own impression of frontman James Hetfield.

The appearance comes amid an eventful year for Dion, who returned to full-length concerts in September after a six-year absence. Her Paris residency marked a significant milestone following her 2022 announcement that she had been diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder that had affected her ability to perform.

entertainment.title: ‘Hold Onto Me,’ Cyprus’ First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a ‘Dogtooth’ Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama
entertainment.summary: Writer-director Myrsini Aristidou's feature debut, starring Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis ('Dogtooth'), tells the story of an 11-year-old girl whose father she has never known comes to town.
entertainment.body:
It’s summertime in Cyprus. Iris, 11, spends her days with her older best friend, Danae. But then she hears that her grandfather has died. Visiting town for his funeral is Iris’ father, Aris, whom she has never known. That is the starting point for Hold Onto Me , the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Can Iris and Aris find a way to connect, even though he is a petty criminal and doesn’t want to take responsibility? Iris doesn’t give up and gets involved in his various schemes, despite warnings from her mother and her older brother. What begins as a stubborn attempt to reconnect slowly unfolds into a fragile bond. But then, Aris’ dark past gets them into trouble. Related Stories TV 'The Remarried Empress' Sets Disney+ and Hulu Record With Biggest Local Original Launch Ever Movies AFM Hot Project: Rosamund Pike to Star in Body Horror 'Feed'

Hold Onto Me , starring newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis ( Dogtooth ), premiered at Sundance, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award. It then became Cyprus’ first-ever international feature film Oscar submission.

Now, the film screens in the Just Film youth and children’s event of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) in Estonia. Cercamon is handling sales.

Lasse Ulvedal Tolbøll was the cinematographer on the Cyprus-Denmark-Greece co-production. The editors were Jenna Mangulad and Aristidou. Aristidou and Monica Nicolaidou produced the film, with Thomas J. Mangan IV and Mark Hollinger as the executive producers and Anders N.U. Berg, Konstantina Stavrianou and Rena Vougioukalou as co-producers.

Aristidou talked to THR about her bittersweet first feature, pairing an unknown as the young girl at the heart of it with the man who played the son in Dogtooth , her desire to make Hold Onto Me feel different and that first-ever Cypriot Oscar submission.

The father-daughter theme is one that the filmmaker has also explored in two shorts. “I feel like this is like a triptych,” Aristidou tells THR . “My first short film called Semele in 2015 is also a father and daughter story and was the first time that I began exploring this theme. Then I did my second short film, Aria , which has a father daughter dynamic again, but with an older daughter – she’s a teenager. They were short, and I wanted to go deeper in this subject matter.”

Hold Onto Me allowed her to do so in feature form, but she wanted it to be surprising and different from other films about similar familial relationships. “I wanted to use the archetypical relationship of father and daughter within a love story,” she explains. “It’s kind of a love story. It’s about two people who don’t know how to be together. They are sort of strangers in the beginning. They meet, then slowly come together, and they end up accepting each other or even loving each other in their own way. And when you set this up within the framework of a father, daughter and their family, it creates a different energy.”

entertainment.summary: Will Estes opens up to TVLine about his Blue Bloods reunion with Donnie Wahlberg - and the possibility of seeing both Jamie and Eddie on Boston Blue.
entertainment.body:
A lot has changed for the Reagan brothers since we last saw them together on "Blue Bloods."

Season 2, Episode 5 of "Boston Blue" marked Will Estes' first appearance as Jamie Reagan since "Blue Bloods" ended its 14-season run in December 2024 — and his reunion with older brother Danny (Donnie Wahlberg) revealed that the distance between them wasn't merely geographical.

Now an NYPD lieutenant and a father to Joey Francis , Jamie arrived in Boston for a police conference harboring some resentment over Danny's decision to leave New York shortly after the birth of his and Eddie's son. (Eddie did not accompany Jamie to Boston, but sent her regards.) What began as a family visit soon turned into a joint investigation involving a diamond heist and a violent family feud, forcing the brothers to confront some lingering tensions of their own.

By the end of the hour, Jamie had come to understand why Danny needed to be in Boston for his son Sean, while Danny acknowledged just how much his departure had hurt his younger brother. Their reconciliation culminated in a heartfelt exchange, with Danny telling Jamie how proud he was of him — not just as a brother and a cop, but now as a father.

In the video interview above — a transcript is provided below — Estes reflects on revisiting Jamie, the real-life emotions behind his reunion with Wahlberg, an unexpected encounter with his former on-screen wife, Vanessa Ray, and whether he'd be open to returning to "Boston Blue."

Seacia Pavao/CBS TVLINE | How long had Jamie's appearance on "Boston Blue" been in the works? Was this something you'd discussed with Donnie and the Brandons as far back as Season 1?

No, it came about more recently than that. I wouldn't say I was waiting by the phone for the call for a whole season, but they reached out to me — Donnie did, and the Brandons — and they were like, "Would you want to be on the show?" And I was like, "Yes! What time? What time are you guys free?" When they told me the story and what they wanted to do with it, I was on board immediately.

entertainment.title: Russell Brand’s jail hell revealed: Vermin-infested cells, violent inmates and drug searches
entertainment.summary: The comedian’s new reality behind bars comes with cramped living quarters, rampant violence, and a strict rules for loved ones hoping to see him.
entertainment.body:
Russell Brand is facing a grim reality behind bars at one of London’s most troubled prisons.

The “Get Him to the Greek” actor, 51, is being held at HMP Wandsworth following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault . Inside, he faces a facility plagued by overcrowding, vermin and violence, according to official watchdog reports.

The Victorian prison is operating at 163% of its normal capacity, compared to a national average of 107%, according the Howard League for Penal Reform .

Wandsworth has 1,457 inmates despite having certified normal accommodation for just 894.

A 2024 report by Wandsworth’s Independent Monitoring Board painted an especially bleak picture of life behind bars, describing conditions inside as “inhumane” and warning of severe risks caused by overcrowding.

The report stated that two men were routinely required to share single-occupancy cells, with some described as “cramped, squalid and featuring broken or missing windows, furniture and fittings.”

Basic necessities were also in short supply, with inmates sometimes going two or three weeks without a full change of clothing. Showers were described as damp, unhygienic and insufficient in number, while poor ventilation allowed mold to return even after refurbishment.

The report also found that crumbling floors provided access for vermin, heating was intermittent because of frequently malfunctioning boilers and summer cell temperatures frequently topped 95 degrees Fahrenheit.

entertainment.title: Before Spider-Man, Sam Raimi Made A '90s Spy Thriller Series That Failed To Take Off
entertainment.summary: Sam Raimi's Hollywood career has been hugely successful, but his work in TV - including one ABC spy thriller - never quite reached the same heights.
entertainment.body:
Set in the wake of the Soviet Union's collapse, "Spy Game" explores the problems that arise when former spies, left with nothing to do, go rogue. Linden Ashby plays Lorne Cash, a retired secret agent who's recruited by Max London (Allison Smith) of the Emergency Counter Hostilities Organization to help reel in these troublemaking spies. Max and Cash are an archetypal odd couple, as Max prefers her fancy gadgets and tech while Cash is more old-school in his approach to spycraft.

The series was clearly made in conversation with classic 1960s shows like "I Spy" and "The Avengers," though it failed to reach the heights achieved by those shows. Variety called the series "loud, unoriginal and unimaginative," while The Los Angeles Times described it as "really bad television on just about every level." The end came quickly, and "Spy Game" was canceled after airing just three episodes.

ABC/YouTube Though "Spy Game" crashed and burned, Sam Raimi has had his hand in several successful TV shows over the years. In the mid-1990s, he created the short-lived superhero show "M.A.N.T.I.S." and produced the horror series "American Gothic," which featured Sarah Paulson in an early role . Around the same time, he produced "Hercules: The Legendary Journeys" and then helped develop and executive produce its more successful spinoff, "Xena: Warrior Princess."

Raimi's interest in Ancient Greek and Roman culture didn't end there. The "Spider-Man" director helped create "Spartacus," the beloved Starz series about gladiators and a slave revolt. His most recent TV creation was "Ash Vs. Evil Dead," the Starz revival of the "Evil Dead" franchise, which he developed alongside his brother, Ivan Raimi. Ivan and Sam's brother, Ted Raimi, starred in that series, in addition to appearing in other Raimi-backed projects like "Spider-Man" and "Xena: Warrior Princess." "Spy Game" co-creator John McNamara has gone on to bigger and better things as well, co-creating the great dark academia series "The Magicians" and serving as an executive producer on "Physical."

Another name now surfacing as one of the Bond mystery men is Nicholas Hoult, a runnerup to Pattinson for Batman years ago.

Pattinson is a favorite of auteurs from Robert Eggers and the Safdie brothers to Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 spy movie Tenet might feel like a Bond audition in hindsight. And more importantly, he worked with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming Dune: Part 3 , which bows Dec. 18 and is said to have gone well for the two men.

The actor is in the midst of the biggest year of his career, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey and as the co-lead of A24 hit The Drama and anchoring the well-reguarded movie Primetime , also from A24. It is the first Bond movie made under the control of Amazon, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. And producing are Spider-Man ‘s Amy Pascal and David Heyman, producer of the Harry Potter movies. A young Pattinson broke out with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire , before gaining global fame a few years later in Twilight .

entertainment.title: Flo Milli Wins Dismissal of Copyright Lawsuit Over ‘Never Lose Me’ Beat Sample
entertainment.summary: A judge ruled that the man who brought the claims did not technically own a beat sampled in the 2023 hit.
entertainment.body:
The Friday (Nov. 6) court ruling, obtained and first reported by Billboard , dismissed the lawsuit without any opportunity to amend. But the case is not over for good; an attorney for the plaintiff said they intend to appeal.

The case was brought last year by Shamar Deal, a Baltimore-based artist who purchased a beat called “Youu” on the rap instrumental marketplace Traktrain in 2019. Deal said that after he paid $200 for a 10-year exclusive license, producer Gerreaux Katana wrongly turned around and relicensed the beat to Babyface Ray and 42 Dugg for their 2023 song “Ron Artest.” Flo Milli then sampled “Ron Artest” on “Never Lose Me,” which peaked at No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The ruling highlights a potential pitfall of online instrumental marketplaces, which have become a common source of beats for aspiring rappers in recent years. As experts have previously told Billboard , casual licensing arrangements can later come back to haunt artists and producers in a business that relies on proper legal paperwork.

Deal’s attorney, Larry Zerner , cited the prevalence of the online beat economy when telling Billboard on Friday that they “respectfully disagree” with Judge Birotte’s decision and plan to appeal it.

“Shamar Deal paid for an exclusive license to this beat,” said Zerner. “The producer listed it for sale as an exclusive, set the price, took the money, and confirmed the sale in his own emails. Shamar also has a contract with the producer that confirms all of these facts. That’s how thousands of independent artists buy beats online every single day, and they deserve to know that the licenses they pay for will hold up. We’re confident the Ninth Circuit will see it that way.”

Reps for Flo Milli and 42 Dugg did not immediately return requests for comment on the ruling.

entertainment.title: 5 Beloved '70s Sitcoms That Don't Hold Up Today
entertainment.summary: There's no shortage of iconic series from the 1970s, but for every sitcom that stands the test of time, you get two that would never fly with viewers today.
entertainment.body:
Television shows will always be products of their times. At a time when topics like desegregation and feminism were only just being openly discussed, a lot of jokes and characterization back then would not land the same way today. The outdated humor that built a lot of those sitcoms would not be appreciated by most television audiences today.

With that in mind, here is a list of five classic sitcoms from the 1970s that simply do not hold up anymore. While the entries on this list are important pieces of television history, they have not withstood the test of time.

ABC One of John Ritter's most memorable roles was Jack Tripper, a cook sharing an apartment with his roommates Janet Wood (Joyce DeWitt) and Chrissy Snow (Suzanne Somers). That concept alone is not alien in today's society, but that was a different case in the 1970s. As such, Jack pretended to be gay so his landlord Mr. Stanley Roper (Norman Fell) would allow an unmarried man to live with two women on his property.

It's easy to see why this sitcom does not hold up today. A man living platonically with two women is nowhere near as scandalous as it was in the 1970s. The "gay panic" that defined Mr. Roper is also outdated in the current era of wider LGBTQ acceptance and pride.

Jack's requirement to "act gay" whenever his landlord is around is also rooted in stereotypes — speaking with a lisp and limping his wrists. In one episode, Mr. Roper wakes up in Jack's bed and immediately panics at the notion that he was in bed with a gay man. Jack even refers to himself as a "Tinkerbell" during this. Obviously, casually offensive humor like this doesn't play well in modern sitcoms.

NBC Few television viewers of the 1970s could turn on "Sanford and Son" without whistling its distinctive theme song from Quincy Jones. The NBC sitcom centered on the short-tempered and sarcastic Fred Sanford (Redd Foxx), who co-owned a Los Angeles junk yard with his son Lamont Sanford (Demond Wilson).

Fred's brash, cantankerous, and bigoted behavior was on par with other angry sitcom fathers like Archie Bunker (Carroll O'Connor). One of his running gags was his constant clashing with his Puerto Rican neighbor Julio Fuentes (Gregory Sierra), whom he'd frequently subject to ethnic insults.

"Sanford and Son" is noteworthy for featuring two black actors in starring roles. But that representation was hardly reflected in the white writers' room. The cast even stepped in sometimes to correct the writing. According to Emmy Magazine , series writer Ted Bergman spoke of a scrapped scene that depicted Fred playing Monopoly with his friend Grady Wilson (Whitman Mayo). "Redd said, 'Black people don't play Monopoly,'" Bergman recalled.

entertainment.title: Why Jane Seymour refuses to leave Malibu despite multiple emergency evacuations
entertainment.summary: Seymour most recently had to evacuate her home in December 2024 with the clothes on her back and a few keepsakes.
entertainment.body:
Jane Seymour is staying put in Malibu — no matter how many times disaster has forced her out .

“No,” Seymour exclusively told Page Six when asked if she’s ever considered leaving the coastal city. “It’s the most beautiful place and the community here is wonderful.”

The actress and QVC Soul to Soul jewelry designer has lived on her Southern California estate for over three decades.

Seymour purchased the 6,326-square-foot oceanfront property for $3.4 million in 1994.

Between Malibu’s rugged geography and powerful Santa Ana winds, the 75-year-old has had to evacuate numerous times over the years because of severe wildfires — including in December 2024, when her home narrowly escaped destruction.

“I hope and pray that my house will be here for a very long time,” Seymour explained. “And I think we’ve personally been through at least half a dozen fires . I’m incredibly grateful to the fire department that ultimately helped us as well. When you live in a place that’s close to nature, you just have to have respect for it.”

Seymour added that she previously took preventive measures to protect her home.

“Quite a long time ago, I ripped out everything in my garden that was not going to be drought healthy and also that would not ignite,” she noted. “I’ve been really, really careful about all that, and I had the fire department here telling me what I should and shouldn’t do, and I did everything I possibly could do, but it’s also the luck of the draw.”

entertainment.title: Jennifer Aniston Guest-Starred In A Vietnam War-Era Quantum Leap Episode
entertainment.summary: Not long before Friends made her one of the biggest TV stars in the world, Jennifer Aniston had a guest role on the time travel adventure show Quantum Leap.
entertainment.body:
